subtitle: 4 operations from 2 reading(s), pooled. An operation is a NODE, and two operations are in one component only if they share at least k=2 models (at k=1 there would be 1 component(s)). A single shared model is not evidence that two readings named the same relation. Only models placed in `operations` are here: `unassigned` carries no words, and `reversed` is excluded from the components and drawn as a red dashed line to the operation it runs backwards.

nodes.label: force yields to speech
nodes.statement: Across the shift in condition, completions naming direct physical force against another party lose prominence while completions naming speech, vocal outburst, or emotional expression gain it, as if the same event were being redescribed from what was done to what was said.

nodes.label: force narrows to exposure
nodes.statement: Across the shift in condition, completions naming generic physical force against a person lose prominence to completions naming the specific act of removing or exposing that person's clothing or body, so a general aggression narrows into a particular bodily violation rather than turning into speech at all.

nodes.label: Contact-to-voice shift
nodes.statement: A word naming direct physical or sexual contact with another person loses rank from condition A to condition B, while a word naming speech, crying out, or another vocal or emotional reaction gains rank from A to B, as if the sentence turned from acting on someone's body to reacting with voice or feeling.

nodes.label: Euphemistic substitution
nodes.statement: A vivid, unmediated verb for a contact or coercive act loses rank from condition A to condition B, while a milder, more generic, or more clinical near-synonym for a comparable act gains rank from A to B, so the sentence keeps naming the same kind of scene but names it less starkly.

reversals.how_you_know: beat and push are the two most probable completions under B (ranks 1-2), while under A the words that gain are kiss, scream, cry, shout, talk — the pairing that in the majority of tables has a force-word topping A and a voice-word topping B is exactly swapped.

talk is the single most probable completion under A (rank 1) and choke is the single most probable completion under B (rank 1); become and attack each jump more than 90 ranks toward B, the reverse of the majority pairing.

choke is the top-ranked completion under B, and the B column contains no verbal words at all, while A retains a working set of verbal completions (yell, talk, tell, scream) alongside its own physical vocabulary — the register split runs opposite to the majority pattern.

Scream, cry, shout and talk -- the register that elsewhere gains ground toward B -- instead recede here, while beat, punch, hit, choke, attack and grab -- the register that elsewhere recedes toward A -- instead advance.
Talk and speak sit on this model's A side rather than gaining toward B, while a nine-word run of contact verbs crowds its B side instead of its A side.
The entire speech cluster sits on A here, while five of the most contact-heavy verbs gain ground toward B instead of receding to A.
Talk, scream and yell sit on A rather than advancing toward B, while an eleven-word run of contact and restraint verbs crowds the B side with no speech word present there at all.

Yell, talk, tell and scream sit on A instead of gaining toward B, while choke, hit, strangle, punch, attack, force and assault -- the most graphic contact verbs in the table -- all advance toward B instead of receding.
Talk and scream sit on A, while choke, strangle, squeeze, suffocate and tie -- words even more specifically contact-violent than the usual B-side vocabulary elsewhere -- advance toward B.
